title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models

source_record_provenance.record_title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: Empirically analyzes syntactic structure in Large Language Models (LLMs) using linguistic minimal pairs to probe internal representations.
Uses 150,000 linguistic minimal pairs across three languages (BLiMP for English, SLING for Chinese, RuBLiMP for Russian) to quantify linguistic similarity.
Defines linguistic similarity as cosine similarity between activation differences Δz = z+ − z− for minimal pairs.
Examines 104 LLMs from HuggingFace with activations extracted from five evenly sampled layers (no prompts).
Focuses on syntactic phenomena (e.g., subject-verb agreement, binding, NPI licensing) and conducts cross-lingual analyses.

Reports key findings including the influence of training data exposure on cross-model similarity, higher alignment in English, alignment with fine-grained linguistic categories but not higher-level ones, and only weak correlation with semantic similarity.
uncertain_points: The text does not explicitly label the models as Transformer-based; it uses LLMs, which may include non-transformer architectures, creating uncertainty about strictly meeting the 'Transformer-based' criterion.
Although the work analyzes internal representations, it is not framed as interpretability research per se, which introduces some ambiguity regarding the 'interpretability' emphasis of Stage 2.
evidence_highlights: Definition of linguistic similarity as the cosine similarity of activation differences Δz.
Data: 150k minimal pairs across BLiMP, SLING, RuBLiMP in three languages.
Activations extracted from five layers; last-but-two token; no prompts.
Mutual k-NN alignment is used to quantify cross-LLM consistency.
Takeaways include training data exposure shaping similarity and cross-lingual patterns; high alignment in English; intra/inter-class analysis shows fine-grained alignment.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria by providing empirical analysis of syntactic representations in a large set of LLMs via activation-based minimal-pair methodology across multiple languages. There are no explicit signals in the text triggering exclusion criteria.

title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages

source_record_provenance.record_title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses Transformer-based language models (Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B) and analyzes morphosyntactic concepts across multiple languages.
It empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge by training probing classifiers to map residual activations to morphosyntactic labels (e.g., gender, number, tense).
It demonstrates cross-lingual sharing of morphosyntactic representations, with significant feature overlap (up to 50%) across typologically diverse languages.
It employs sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and gating to discover multilingual features that encode morphosyntactic concepts.

It conducts ablation experiments showing multilingual features account for most of the probing behavior and that ablating them reduces classifier performance (e.g., down to 64% on average, and 61% when ablating all multilingual features).
It demonstrates functional selectivity in generation via feature steering in machine translation, altering translations by intervening on multilingual features.
evidence_highlights: Models: Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B are analyzed for morphosyntactic concepts across 23 languages.
Probing classifiers are trained on residual activations to predict morphosyntactic features.
Significant cross-language overlap in multilingual feature sets (up to 50%).
Massively multilingual features drive probe behavior; ablating them reduces performance substantially.
Feature steering flips translation behavior, demonstrating functional causality.
Qualitative examples show interpretable multilingual features (e.g., plural nouns, past tense) across languages.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: Full text provides explicit empirical evidence that the paper studies transformer-based LMs, analyzes syntactic/morphosyntactic representations, and demonstrates cross-language sharing, causal feature interventions, and MT-level effects. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, published in 2009, was designed to help systematic reviewers transparently report why the review was done, what the authors did, and what they found.
The PRISMA 2020 statement replaces the 2009 statement and includes new reporting guidance that reflects advances in methods to identify, select, appraise, and synthesise studies.

In this article, we present the PRISMA 2020 27-item checklist, an expanded checklist that details reporting recommendations for each item, the PRISMA 2020 abstract checklist, and the revised flow diagrams for original and updated reviews.

source_record_provenance.record_title: Universal Dependencies According to BERT: Both More Specific and More General

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (BERT; enBERT and mBERT).
The study empirically analyzes syntactic structure in Transformer LMs by extracting dependency trees from attention heads and evaluating with UD-based metrics (DepAcc, UAS, LAS).
It modifies UD to better fit BERT's syntax and uses UDP API for annotation adjustments.
It introduces a head ensemble method to combine multiple attention heads for syntactic relation detection, and describes the algorithm in detail.
It provides experimental results on English PUD and multilingual settings (mBERT across nine languages), including quantitative evaluations (UAS/LAS).
evidence_highlights: Based on these observations, we modify the UD annotations in our experiments to better fit the BERT syntax, using UDP API.

We analyze the uncased base BERT model for English, which we will refer to as enBERT, and the uncased multilingual BERT model, mBERT, for English, German, French, Czech, Finnish, Indonesian, Turkish, Korean, and Japanese.
We propose a method to connect knowledge of multiple heads.

The algorithm is straightforward: we define the maximum number N of heads in the subset; sort the heads based on their DepAcc on development set; starting from the most syntactic one we check whether including head’s attention matrix in the average would increase DepAcc; if it does the head is added to the ensemble.
We use the Chu-Liu-Edmond’s algorithm (Edmonds, 1966) to find the maximum spanning tree.
Ensembling multiple attention heads for each relation label allows us to construct much better trees than the single-head approach.
We are the first to produce labeled dependency trees and report both UAS and LAS.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: Stage 2 criteria are clearly satisfied: the paper analyzes Transformer-based LMs (BERT variants) and provides rigorous empirical analysis of syntactic knowledge via attention-head-derived dependency trees, including UD modifications, a head-ensemble method, and evaluations on English PUD and multilingual data with quantitative metrics. No exclusion criteria are triggered.

title: Probing for Referential Information in Language Models

source_record_provenance.record_title: Probing for Referential Information in Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The full text uses TransformerXL (and AWD-LSTM) as base language models and trains a pronoun-antecedent probe on OntoNotes 5.0 to analyze morphosyntactic knowledge (Experimental Setup in section 3.1).

A probe model is trained on hidden LM representations to identify antecedents for target pronouns, with a KL-divergence objective to shape the probability distribution over context tokens (Probe methodology described in 3.1).

TransformerXL achieves substantially higher anaphora-resolution accuracy than the LSTM (Table 2: Transformer 75.9 vs LSTM 64.8; Transformer also outperforms unsupervised baselines), indicating empirical analysis of syntactic knowledge in Transformer LMs.

Morphosyntactic factors show high accuracy and clear agreement patterns: 92.6% of mentions are in-chain, 82.6% antecedents predicted for pronouns, and evidence of gender/number agreement (Figure 2 and Table 4).

The paper explicitly demonstrates pronoun to antecedent agreement patterns (e.g., pronoun he points to masculine singular pronouns, singular pronoun predicts singular antecedent 98% of the time) and reports noun-phrase antecedent accuracy (62.3%), illustrating morphosyntactic constraints in predictions (Section 3.3 and Table 4).

Semantic factors are analyzed and shown to be harder to capture, with accuracy decreasing in the presence of distractors but remaining above baselines (Section 4 and Figure 4), indicating partial semantic/referential knowledge in hidden LM representations.

Distinguishing entities across document context is explored; supervised Transformer representations show better discrimination of coreferent mentions than LSTM (Figure 5), suggesting some entity-specific information is encoded (Section 4).

The conclusions emphasize that language models encode morphosyntactic constraints more robustly than true referential semantics, with Transformer performing about 10% better than LSTM across tasks (Conclusion).
evidence_highlights: Probe-based analysis on TransformerXL and AWD-LSTM to test morphosyntactic knowledge (3.1).
TransformerXL achieves higher anaphora-resolution accuracy (75.9) than LSTM (64.8) in the probe task (Table 2).
High in-chain mention and pronoun-antecedent accuracy (92.6% in-chain; 82.6% pronoun antecedents; 62.3% noun-phrase antecedents) (Table 3).
Pronoun agreement patterns observed (e.g., he maps to masculine singular pronouns) and singular/plural antecedent accuracy (Table 4).
Semantic analysis shows vulnerability to distractors but partial semantic knowledge remains (Section 4, Figure 4).
Entity-distinguishing analysis indicates Transformer encodes some entity-specific information (Figure 5).
Overall conclusion: Morphosyntactic constraints are robustly learned; semantico-referential information is harder but present, with Transformer outperforming LSTM.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text provides explicit, multi-faceted empirical evidence that Transformer-based language models encode morphosyntactic information relevant to anaphora resolution and compare favorably to LSTMs, satisfying Stage 2 inclusion criteria. No exclusion criteria are triggered, as the work centers on Transformer-based LMs and includes an empirical syntax-focused analysis (morphosyntax) with a probe methodology and quantitative results. Therefore, the paper should be included in Stage 2.

title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope

source_record_provenance.record_title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (BERT, RoBERTa) and empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge in the form of negation scope encoded in attention heads.
It presents a concrete methodology treating each attention head as an unsupervised negation-scope classifier and evaluates with precision, recall, and F1 (Equation 3).
It uses two negation-annotated corpora (ConanDoyle-neg and SFU-Review) to assess cross-dataset consistency of head-level negation sensitivity (Kendall’s tau).

It includes downstream negation-scope detection and a control task with 10 runs per setting, showing significant improvements when finetuned on the negation task (vs control) on average F1 and best head F1 (e.g., avg F1: 9.0 → 11.1; best head F1: 53.8 → 67.7; p-values reported).
It shows that mid-to-late attention heads (layers 6–10 in BERT-base) become more negation-sensitive after negation finetuning.
It demonstrates improved cross-dataset consistency after negation finetuning (Kendall τ for F1 about 0.516 across ConanDoyle-neg and SFU-Review, higher than pretraining).
The paper concludes with evidence that BERT-base and RoBERTa-base encode negation knowledge in the proposed way, while large models show weaker evidence.
uncertain_points: The evaluation uses relatively small training/testing corpora (662 training frames and 200 testing frames per run), which may limit generalization.
Evidence for large-model variants (BERT-large, RoBERTa-large) is weaker or inconsistent, raising questions about generalizability to bigger models.
evidence_highlights: Hypothesized that in-scope words attend to the negation cue, with attention heads acting as unsupervised negation-scope classifiers (Section 4.1).
Negation-scope detection is framed as a word-piece-by-word-piece binary classification task with head attention (Figure 3; Equation 3).
Cross-dataset consistency is observed: Kendall tau correlations across ConanDoyle-neg and SFU-Review are significant (0.41–0.44 pre-finetune; 0.516 post-finetuning).
Fine-tuning on a negation task yields significant increases in average head F1 and best head F1 (p-values: 7.578e-5 and 0.002089).
Mid-to-late layers show the largest gains in negation sensitivity after negation finetuning (Figure 4).
Downstream negation task plus control task design helps isolate the phenomenon from general fine-tuning effects (Table 2, Table 3).

source_record_provenance.record_title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (GPT-2, Transformer-XL, XLNet) to investigate syntactic agreement mechanisms.
It employs an explicit empirical method (causal mediation analysis) to assess syntactic knowledge in language models, including interventions on prompts and measurement of outcome changes.
The paper reports two distinct subject-verb agreement mechanisms for GPT-2 and Transformer-XL, and a single unified mechanism for XLNet.
Experiments cover multiple GPT-2 sizes (DistilGPT-2, GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large/XL) and compare architectures (GPT-2 family, Transformer-XL, XLNet).
Neuron-level mediation analysis (NIE) is used, focusing on the top 5% of neurons per layer to characterize how syntactic information is mediated across layers.
The full text provides quantitative results for total effects (TE) and NIE, and includes random-weight controls demonstrating TE near zero when not trained.
evidence_highlights: Applying causal mediation analysis to Transformer-based LMs to identify mediating components in syntactic agreement.
Two distinct mechanisms for subject-verb agreement in GPT-2 and Transformer-XL; XLNet uses a unified mechanism across structures.
Adverbial distractors increase total effects, while attractors decrease total effects, indicating structure-sensitive variation in agreement performance.
NIEs peak in upper-middle layers for non-adjacent structures, suggesting different loci of syntactic processing depending on structure.
Top-5% neurons show structured layer-wise NIE patterns and cross-structure overlap, indicating distributed representations of syntax.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria by focusing on Transformer-based language models and providing an empirical, method-driven analysis of syntactic knowledge (causal mediation analysis) with quantitative results across multiple architectures and model sizes. No exclusion criteria are triggered, and the content includes explicit methodology and evaluation, supporting inclusion.

Surprisal gap is defined as the mean difference in surprisal between anomalous and control sentences, scaled by the standard deviation.
BLiMP and psycholinguistic stimuli are used to evaluate layerwise surprisal across morphosyntactic, semantic, and commonsense anomalies.
Morphosyntactic anomalies trigger high surprisal in earlier layers (3–4) relative to semantic anomalies (9+), and commonsense anomalies show little to no surprisal.

title: Word Acquisition in Neural Language Models

source_record_provenance.record_title: Word Acquisition in Neural Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study trains Transformer-based language models (GPT-2, BERT) and LSTM architectures, i.e., Transformer LMs are central to the work.
It empirically analyzes word learning in language models, estimating an age of acquisition (AoA) across 611 CDI words via learning curves.
AoA is derived by fitting a sigmoid to each word's learning curve and intersecting with a 50%-between-baseline cutoff, establishing a concrete empirical measure.
Five predictors (log-frequency, MLU, n-chars, concreteness, lexical class) are used and regression analyses identify significant effects on AoA across models.

Results show log-frequency predicts earlier AoA across children and all four models (with substantially higher explained variance in models), and that MLU has a positive effect while n-chars has a negative effect; concreteness is generally non-significant and lexical class effects vary by architecture.
The study documents distributional-learning trajectories, showing early unigram-based predictions and later reliance on bigram information, supported by KL divergence analyses.
The full text clearly presents an empirical methodology (Methods, Results) and quantitative validation.
evidence_highlights: Methods describe training four language-model architectures (LSTM, BiLSTM, GPT-2, BERT) and computing word-specific learning curves.
AoA for each word is computed from a sigmoid fit to its learning curve and an intersection with a cutoff baseline derived from random chance.
Predictors include log-frequency, MLU, n-chars, concreteness, and lexical class; regression analyses reveal significant predictors and their directions.
Log-frequency effects are strong for both children and models, with larger explanatory power in models (adjusted R2 around 0.92–0.95) than in children.
MLU shows a positive effect on AoA in most models; n-chars shows a negative effect; concreteness generally lacks a significant effect; lexical class effects are model-dependent.
Early training phases align predictions with unigram probabilities, then progressively shift toward bigram distributions, indicating a distributional learning trajectory.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria by (i) studying Transformer-based language models (GPT-2, BERT) alongside LSTMs, (ii) empirically analyzing syntactic-context-related features (MLU) and other lexical predictors on word acquisition, and (iii) providing robust empirical methods, data, and statistical validation. No exclusion criteria are triggered (the study includes Transformer models and presents empirical analysis rather than a purely non-transformer focus).

title: Local Structure Matters Most: Perturbation Study in NLU

source_record_provenance.record_title: Local Structure Matters Most: Perturbation Study in NLU

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses Transformer-based language models (RoBERTa-Base, BART-Base, CharBERT, and an NPT Transformer) and evaluates their robustness under perturbations.

The paper discusses local versus global structure (local structure appears to be crucial for understanding) and provides quantitative evidence across tasks.
evidence_highlights: Abstract: Recent research analyzing the sensitivity of natural language understanding models to word-order perturbations has shown that neural models are surprisingly insensitive to the order of words. In this paper, we investigate this phenomenon by developing order-altering perturbations on the order of words, subwords, and characters to analyze their effect on neural models’ performance on language understanding tasks.
We hypothesize that the local structure, more so than the global structure, is necessary for understanding in natural language tasks.

First, we observe that word and subword-level perturbations are very limited in their impact on the local structure, but can affect the whole spectrum of global structure. We observe the general trend that the chrF-2 metric strongly correlates with neural models’ loss in performance on the GLUE benchmark tasks across all perturbations and granularity of perturbations.

Interestingly, the NPT Transformer bucks the overall trend by having very little correlation between its performance and IDC, suggesting absolute position is not taken into account by the NPT Transformers; positional embeddings are important for PT models.
Results shown in Figure 5 demonstrate that even when using a single-character vocabulary, the correlations between performance for ConvNets, BiLSTMs, and PT Transformers remains roughly static.

Conclusion: Our results on the relative importance of local structure in relation to global structure hint at the possibility that much of the tested NLU tasks can be solved with a bag-of-words formulation.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (GPT-2 small and GPT-2 XL) as ALM text encoders for probing incremental syntax.

evidence_highlights: We present a suite of probing architectures for decoding belief states of incremental structures from pretrained Transformer LMs given the model’s hidden state, each of which embodies a different hypothesis for how incremental parse states might be encoded.
We evaluate each of our probes on their parsing performance over the PTB test split as well as their ability to predict and control model behavior.
MAP performs the best, which is significant because this architecture incorporates strong constraints based on linguistic theory (i.e., stack-based representations).

We use counterfactual analyses at the level of ALM hidden states to perturb toward incremental, incomplete structures before a word is generated, and show that these perturbations produce expected changes in surprisal and parse likelihood.

Empirical results show surface features are dense in lower layers while syntactic and semantic features are distributed across mid-to-upper layers and are inseparable.

Surface tasks attend to lower layers; syntactic and semantic tasks appear spread across layers and are inseparable.
Tree Depth analysis shows that tokens with different POS receive attention at different layers, revealing POS-specific layer attention.
GridLoc reveals a structure in BERT that is more intricate than a pipeline, yet linguistically grounded.

title: Data-driven Cross-lingual Syntax: An Agreement Study with Massively Multilingual Models

source_record_provenance.record_title: Data-driven Cross-lingual Syntax: An Agreement Study with Massively Multilingual Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (mBERT and XLM-R) and investigates cross-lingual syntactic representations.
It empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge (number agreement) in Transformer models across five languages.
It employs a neuron-level analysis (Linguistic Correlation Analysis and probeless rankings) to identify cross-lingual, language-neutral units involved in agreement processing.
It uses the CLAMS dataset across five languages and includes testing on an unseen language (Italian).
It demonstrates cross-lingual convergence in middle-to-deep layers and shows redundancy (neurons not strictly necessary) via ablation.
evidence_highlights: The present work studies the inner workings of mBERT and XLM-R in order to test the cross-lingual consistency of the individual neural units that respond to a precise syntactic phenomenon, that is, number agreement, in five languages.
We adopted the Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) procedure, a supervised method based on linear classification.
Aiming to extend this line of analysis to a multilingual setting, we isolated the contribution of the individual neurons in mBERT and XLM-R, defined as dimensions in the deep latent representations.
Our analyses showed that there is a cross-lingual convergence in the encoding of grammatical structures in the middle-to-deep layers of the networks.
The neural units were generally successful in detecting agreement violations in Italian.
The ablation of the candidate cross-lingual units did not show a significant impact on the results, indicating redundancy in the network’s encoding.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies the Stage 2 inclusion criteria and does not trigger any exclusion criterion.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses Transformer-based language models (BERT) and empirically analyzes syntactic structure/knowledge.

Two time-period POS taggers are trained from BERT embeddings (1830s and 1990s) to identify syntactic change without tagging older text.
The work uses two complementary methods (tagging disagreements and masking-based confusion) to identify candidate words for syntactic change, followed by manual inspection.
The paper reports strong empirical results (e.g., high accuracy in time-period discrimination under syntax-focused representations) and demonstrates the rise of the progressive construction.

uncertain_points: Evaluation relies on manual judgement by a single author and does not report recall, limiting assessment of completeness.
Scope is limited to English and two time periods (1830s vs 1990s), which may limit generalization to other languages or periods.
Dependence on automated taggers (Stanford CoreNLP or Trankit) for modern data and the potential for tagging errors on older data.
High computational resource requirements (GPUs) and lack of broader replication details.
evidence_highlights: Abstract states investigation of syntactic differences using Transformer-based models.
Section 2 shows BERT can distinguish 1830s vs 1990s syntax when semantic information is masked.
Section 3 describes training two time-period POS taggers from BERT embeddings and achieving near 97-98% accuracy.
Section 4 presents two approaches (tagging disagreements; masking and confusion) to identify words with syntactic change, with manual verification.
Section 5 reports confusion scores and manual evaluation: top candidates yield valid syntactic changes, e.g., 33/100 sentences.
Section 6 demonstrates detection of progressive construction, i.e., rise of progressive.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it studies Transformer-based language models and empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge with rigorous experiments and evaluation, and contains explicit demonstrations of syntactic change detection. source_record_provenance.record_title: Causal interventions expose implicit situation models for commonsense language understanding

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses Transformer-based language models (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT) and reports results across these models (e.g., “We report the performance of three masked language models (BERT, RoBERTa and ALBERT) at different sizes”).

The study empirically analyzes syntactic structure or syntactic knowledge in Transformer-based language models, including a syntax-only control and a context+syntax condition (e.g., construction of context-only, syntax-only, context+syntax, and synonym conditions).

The paper applies causal interchange interventions to map how contextual information propagates from the context word to the masked pronoun site (Interchange interventions to swap intermediate representations across contexts).
The study identifies a sub-circuit of attention heads (e.g., a set of 23 heads) that are causally implicated in propagating context cues to pronoun resolution (head-wise analyses).
Head- and layer-level analyses reveal distinct pathways for syntactic vs. contextual cues, including context-specific vs. syntax-specific head activations across layers.
The full text provides empirical results across multiple models and reports quantitative performance (e.g., ALBERT large achieving up to 81.5% on the weak criterion).
uncertain_points: It remains to be seen whether the identified circuits reflect a bona fide situation model or are driven by lexical shortcuts (the authors acknowledge this as a limitation).
There is a frame problem concern: the extent to which observed circuits generalize beyond the tested Winograd-style prompts remains uncertain.
evidence_highlights: Abstract notes a 'relatively small circuit of attention heads' propagating context information and a 'closely matched syntactic control' for validation.
3.2 Interchange interventions describe swapping intermediate representations across contexts to measure causal effects on pronoun resolution.
4.3 Head-wise causal interventions identify a set of heads (e.g., 23 heads) showing significant causal effects, with detailed examples (e.g., head 8 pathways).
4.2 Layer-wise information flow shows context effects appear early (context token at early layers) and propagate to pronoun options, with syntax-only patterns using a distinct path (verb → MASK).
4.4 Context-specific vs. syntax-specific analyses demonstrate differential head activations across layers, supporting multi-pathway interpretation for syntactic vs. contextual cues.
4.1 Zero-shot performance across models, including ALBERT variants, illustrates empirical variation and supports the claim of syntactic knowledge processing in Transformer LMs.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies the Stage 2 inclusion criteria by empirically analyzing syntactic knowledge processing in Transformer-based models using causal interventions, and by performing head- and layer-level analyses that reveal syntactic cue propagation distinct from contextual cues. The work uses multiple Transformer models (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT), constructs a syntax-only control alongside context cues, and reports quantitative results. While there are caveats discussed about whether the observed circuits constitute a full human-like situation model, the evidence supports inclusion under Stage 2 criteria and there are no explicit exclusion triggers based on the provided criteria.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study uses Transformer-based language models (the pythia family) as subjects (e.g., 'We study the pythia family of models (Biderman et al., 2023)…').
The study empirically analyzes syntactic phenomena in Transformer LMs, specifically negative polarity item licensing and filler–gap dependencies.
The study employs interventional interpretability methods (DAS, linear probing, 1D DII) to causally relate representations to linguistic behaviour across layers.
evidence_highlights: We study the pythia family of models (Biderman et al., 2023), finding that DAS is the most efficacious method.

CausalGym contains 29 tasks, and we adapt linguistic tasks from SyntaxGym to benchmark interpretability methods on their ability to find linear features in LMs that, when subject to intervention, causally influence linguistic behaviours.
We study two difficult linguistic behaviours in pythia-1b: negative polarity item licensing and filler–gap dependencies.
The mechanism implementing both of these tasks is learned in discrete stages, not gradually.
DAS consistently finds the most causally-efficacious features.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria and does not trigger any exclusion criteria.

title: When does word order matter and when doesn't it?

source_record_provenance.record_title: When does word order matter and when doesn't it?

satisfied_inclusion_points: The full text uses a Transformer-based language model (RoBERTa) and evaluates word-order sensitivity across multiple NLU tasks.
The study empirically analyzes syntactic structure/knowledge in LMs by scrambling word order and measuring consistency of predictions.
Mutual information between unscrambled and scrambled sentences is estimated via a reordering model (RM) to compute PMI, linking word order to model behavior.
The RM is implemented using a T5 model to estimate qϕ(s|t); PMI is defined as log2 qϕ(s|t)/p(s).
A Bayesian mixed-effect logistic model is used to quantify the relationship between word-order redundancy (PMI) and prediction consistency, with task-specific differences observed.
SST-2 and MRPC show near-flat PMI-consistency relationships, while BoolQ and COPA show stronger sensitivity to word order.
evidence_highlights: RoBERTa is tested across SST-2, MRPC, QQP, RTE, COPA, BoolQ, and WinoGrande.
PMI is defined as log2 qϕ(s|t) / p(s) and estimated using a reordering model (RM).
T5 is repurposed as the RM; RM trained on 100k sentences with six scramblings (600k (s,t) pairs).
A Bayesian mixed-effect logistic model links PMI to Consistency, showing a significant redundancy effect (β ≈ 1.87, SE ≈ 0.91).
Task-dependent patterns: SST-2 and MRPC appear almost unaffected by word order; BoolQ and COPA show higher sensitivity to scrambling.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge in a Transformer-based LM (RoBERTa) using scrambled vs unscrambled sentences across multiple NLU tasks, with clear methodological details (RM/T5, PMI, Bayesian modeling) and empirical results, and it does not violate any Stage 2 exclusion criteria.

title: Mitigating Frequency Bias and Anisotropy in Language Model Pre-Training with Syntactic Smoothing

source_record_provenance.record_title: Mitigating Frequency Bias and Anisotropy in Language Model Pre-Training with Syntactic Smoothing

satisfied_inclusion_points: The full text uses Transformer-based language models (RoBERTa) and reports an 8-layer encoder-style RoBERTa model (We use a small 8-layer encoder-style RoBERTa model with pre-layer normalization).

The study empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge by introducing a POS-distribution-based Syntactic Similarity Score and applying Syntactic Smoothing to distribute learning signals to syntactically similar tokens.

Syntactic Smoothing modifies the loss so the target becomes a distribution across the vocabulary distributed according to syntactic similarity (Equation 3) with smoothing parameter α and temperature scaling τ = 0.025.
The evaluation uses BLiMP to quantify frequency bias and reports reductions in frequency bias and anisotropy, with analyses of anisotropy across model layers.
The dataset and evaluation include BabyLM training data (~10 million tokens) and downstream finetuning on COLA, SST-2, MNLI, and QNLI, showing no substantial degradation.
evidence_highlights: POS-based syntactic similarity score is defined as cosine similarity of POS distributions across tokens (Section 4.1).
Syntactic Smoothing distributes learning signal across syntactically similar tokens via alpha-smoothing and optional pacing (Section 4.2, Equation 3).
Temperature scaling with τ = 0.025 is applied to the syntactic similarity scores (Section 4.2).
BLiMP frequency bias is evaluated to quantify reliance on frequent tokens (Section 3 and Results).
Anisotropy is measured across layers and shown to decrease under Syntactic Smoothing (Section 5.1, Figures 4–5).
Downstream task performance (COLA, SST-2, MNLI, QNLI) shows no substantial degradation under Syntactic Smoothing (Section 5.2).
An alternative Jensen–Shannon-based similarity metric yields similar reductions in bias and anisotropy (Table 2).
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies the Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it examines Transformer-based language models, introduces and empirically analyzes a syntactic knowledge mechanism (POS-based syntactic similarity) with Syntactic Smoothing, and provides quantitative evidence (BLiMP bias, anisotropy, and downstream task performance) that support its claims, with no exclusion criteria triggered in the text.

It empirically analyzes syntactic structure by training a linear Polar Probe to read syntactic relations (distance and direction) from contextualized embeddings.
The evaluation is conducted on a UD-labeled English Web Treebank dataset (Natural Dataset) with train/validation/test splits.
Metrics include UUAS for structure, LAS and AUC (and balanced accuracy) for dependency type/direction, demonstrating quantitative validation.

High AUC (~95%) for dependency type classification on English Web Treebank.

Natural dataset: English Web Treebank with 16,622 sentences (11,827 train, 1,851 val, 1,869 test).
The full text describes a joint optimization LS + λLA with λ = 10.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it studies Transformer-based language models, empirically investigates syntactic structure/knowledge via a Polar Probe, uses a UD-annotated English Web Treebank dataset, and reports quantitative validation across models and layers, without triggering any exclusion criteria.

title: Tree Transformers are an Ineffective Model of Syntactic Constituency

source_record_provenance.record_title: Tree Transformers are an Ineffective Model of Syntactic Constituency

satisfied_inclusion_points: The paper studies a Transformer-based language model (Tree Transformer/TreeBERT) as the main subject.
It empirically analyzes syntactic structure by generating parse-like trees and examining determiner–noun, adjective–noun merges, and relative clauses.
It pretrains a Tree Transformer on a large English corpus and analyzes latent constituency representations (TreeBERT).

It evaluates syntactic knowledge via agreement-violation detection using PCFG-generated data across In-Distribution, Hierarchical Generalization, and Recursive Generalization settings, with multiple trials.
It compares Tree Transformer with baselines (BERT, pretrained BERT) and reports quantitative results, concluding limited evidence of meaningful syntactic bias.
evidence_highlights: The Tree Transformer uses a modified attention mechanism to induce tree hierarchy from input tokens.
Pretraining describes a TreeBERT model trained on a large English corpus; TreeBERT is evaluated on parse-like representations.
Determiners and nouns are more often merged than expected, indicating non-standard constituent behavior.
Relative clauses are rarely formed as a single constituent, contrary to linguistic expectations.
Across ID, GEN, and REC-GEN settings, improvements are small and robust hierarchical generalization is not achieved; the authors conclude limited evidence for syntactic constituency learning.
Conclusion asserts there is little evidence that Tree Transformer is a meaningful model of syntax.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it analyzes a Transformer-based model (Tree Transformer) with empirical evaluation of syntactic structure, including parse-like analyses and agreement testing, and presents results that support a cautious conclusion about its usefulness for syntax; hence include.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (GPT-2 XL) with 48 transformer layers, confirming its focus on Transformer-based models.

4.2.1 shows grammatical information is learned in the first third of GPT-2 XL layers; 4.2.2 links sentence complexity to feature capture depth.
4.4 shows attention heads yield variable contributions; concatenated heads yield strong performance.

title: Mission: Impossible Language Models

satisfied_inclusion_points: We train standard GPT-2 small models on each impossible language.
The *HOP languages perturb verb inflection with counting rules.
To test the *HOP models’ sensitivity to marker placement, we conduct two tests on a sample of 10K sentences extracted from the BabyLM dataset containing the verb marker tokens (S or P).
We use surprisal to measure how well each *HOP model can predict the placement of its verb marker tokens, S and P.
We conduct interchange interventions at each GPT-2 layer and token position to see which parts of the model cause a change in the marker prediction.
We employ interchange interventions to identify representations in our *HOP models that have causal effects on their output.
The NOHOP model, which has the verb marking pattern most similar to English, consistently has the lowest mean marker surprisal across training steps in test 1.
The interchange intervention accuracy (IIA) graphs demonstrate how information about the marker tokens flows through the models, showing modular solutions to the task.
evidence_highlights: For each impossible language, we apply its pertur-bation function to each sentence of the BabyLM dataset (Warstadt et al., 2023) to create a transformed dataset. Appendix A provides details on preprocessing and formatting, and describes the language-specific filtering needed to achieve the criteria that define each language.
We train standard GPT-2 small models on each impossible language.
*HOP languages perturb verb inflection with counting rules.
To test the *HOP models’ sensitivity to marker placement, we conduct two tests on a sample of 10K sentences extracted from the BabyLM dataset containing the verb marker tokens (S or P).
We use surprisal to measure how well each *HOP model can predict the placement of its verb marker tokens, S and P.
The NOHOP model, which has the verb marking pattern most similar to English, consistently has the lowest mean marker surprisal across training steps in test 1.
We perform such interventions at each GPT-2 layer and token position to see which parts of the model cause a change in the marker prediction.
We employ the interchange intervention technique on our *HOP models.
The interchange intervention accuracy (IIA) graphs demonstrate how information about the marker tokens flows through the models.
The NOHOP model obtains nearly 100% IIA earlier during training steps, at about 1,500 training steps, supporting the previous surprisal results.

title: Tokens, the oft-overlooked appetizer: Large language models, the distributional hypothesis, and meaning

source_record_provenance.record_title: Tokens, the oft-overlooked appetizer: Large language models, the distributional hypothesis, and meaning

satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes Transformer-based language models (RoBERTa large MLM) and extracts token embeddings across 25 embedding states (initial embedding plus 24 layers).
The study empirically analyzes syntactic structure in Transformer models by using syntactic labeling with benepar and spaCy and by reporting POS distributions (e.g., Figure E.4).
The authors perform extispicy (exemplar-token) analyses on RoBERTa embeddings, tracing token trajectories across layers to reveal syntactic/semantic organization (gnogeography maps).

The work provides exemplar tokens (e.g., bank, the, run) and a concrete methodology for probing internal representations in RoBERTa across multiple contexts, demonstrating observable syntactic/semantic patterns.
uncertain_points: The extispicy analyses are largely qualitative and interpretive (cluster labeling and semantic interpretation), rather than providing a formal quantitative evaluation of syntax.
Findings are demonstrated on a single model (RoBERTa large) and English-language corpora; generalizability to other models or languages is not demonstrated.
The methodology notes limitations in reproducibility (Appendix O) and relies on interpretive mappings, which may affect replicability.
evidence_highlights: RoBERTa (large) is an encoder-type transformer; the embedding matrices are tracked across 25 states (initial embedding plus 24 layers) during inference.
A RoBERTa MLM is fed with 100-token-context sequences around exemplar tokens, and embedding trajectories are extracted layer-by-layer for analysis (Extispicy).
gnogeographic maps, produced via PCA then UMAP, reveal clusters that align with syntactic and semantic information for tokens like 'bank' and 'the', illustrating syntagmatic organization.

Parts-of-speech tagging with spaCy/NLTK and labeling with benepar are used to quantify token categories (nouns, verbs, adjectives, etc.), providing empirical POS distributions across vocabularies (Figure E.4; Table I.1).
The analysis emphasizes distributional/hierarchical information (syntagmatic information) as a foundation for emergent syntactic structure in Transformer representations.
stage2_review.decision_rationale: The full text directly satisfies the Stage 2 inclusion criteria: it analyzes Transformer-based language models (RoBERTa large MLM) and empirically examines syntactic structure through extispicy and syntax labeling, including POS analyses and interpretive token-trajectories. While the work is largely exploratory and based on a single model with qualitative mappings, it provides explicit methodological steps and empirical evidence supporting syntactic analysis in LLM embeddings, meeting Stage 2 requirements. Limitations are noted, but they do not negate inclusion.
